fieldMarks: Typically green, but can be brown or nearly black; some adults turn orange or pink seasonally
Row of spikes down the centre of neck, back and upper tail; dark black rings on the tail
Mature males have heavy jowls and a much larger dewlap (throat fan) than females
Males reach over 5 ft and 17 lb; females usually stay under 7 lb
behavior: Mostly arboreal; excellent swimmer that can submerge up to four hours
Mainly herbivorous: leaves, flowers and fruit; adults also take bird eggs and carrion
Males signal with head-bobbing and dewlap extension
Not cold-hardy, which limits establishment northward
habitat: Trees, shrubs and ground in forest, urban, suburban and agricultural settings; lives in burrows and culverts in cleared areas of Florida.
range: Native from Central America through tropical South America and some Caribbean islands. Introduced in southern Florida (mostly the southern half of the peninsula, commonest near the coast), Puerto Rico and Hawaii. Not native to Canada.
